newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African MPs demand review of rhino horn move.
newsitem.headline: S.African MPs demand review of rhino horn move.

text.p: South African legislators demanded on Tuesday that President Nelson Mandela's cabinet review its decision to push for legal trade in rhino horn and to support limited trading in ivory.

Members of a parliamentary oversight committee told Pallo Jordan, minister of environmental affairs and tourism, that the cabinet had taken positions on next week's meeting of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) without consulting the public.

"This committee was not consulted, and of all the stakeholders in South Africa, I don't remember anybody who says 'Yes, I've been part of the process'...We feel that it is a decision that has been rushed," committee chairwoman Gwen Mahlangu told Jordan.

The minister said he would take the committee's concerns to a cabinet meeting on Wednesday but added he backed the proposal, drafted by the parastatal Natal Parks Board conservation group, to seek legal trade in the horns of white rhino.

"As long as the market demand is there, people are going to go after the rhino. How to find a way that is going to address the market demand and at the same time conserve the rhino? That is the attempt that is being made here," Jordan said.

"It might be a disastrous failure, but what we are facing now is a disaster anyway...The Natal Parks Board has come up with a possible solution. The status quo is not resulting in the saving of the rhino, it is being hunted and killed," he said.

All trade in rhino products is now banned by CITES in an effort to halt poaching that has driven the two African species, known as black and white rhino, close to extinction in countries other than South Africa.
A Natal Parks Board breeding programme has resulted in white rhino reaching healthy numbers in South Africa, where poaching is virtually unknown and trophy hunting of the species is allowed.
Rhino horn is ground to powder for medicinal use in Asia and is carved into handles for traditionial daggers in Yemen.

On the ivory trade, Jordan said South Africa had decided in the interests of regional solidarity to support a proposal by Namibia, Zimbabwe and Botswana that ivory and hides from their elephants be traded legally.

He said all members of the Southern African Development Community (SADC) -- Angola, Botswana, Lesotho, Swaziland, Namibia, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Mauritius, Malawi, South Africa, Mozambique and Tanzania -- were expected to support the proposal at the CITES meeting which starts in Zimbabwe on Monday.

Some animal welfare groups have complained that any easing of the total bans on trade in rhino and elephant products will encourage poachers and be the death knell for those animals remaining in countries north of Zimbabwe.
